description: Which rule wins when styles collide: specificity, the cascade, and inheritance.

screens.body:
Two rules target the same element and set the same property. Only one can win — the browser needs a tiebreaker.

That tiebreaker system is the cascade: a set of rules that picks the winner based on specificity first, then order.

Understanding it turns "why won't this style apply?!" from a mystery into a five-second diagnosis.

options: The cascade — specificity first, then order
A random pick by the browser
check.question: What decides which conflicting rule wins?

screens.heading: When rules collide
screens.keyPoint: The cascade picks one winner: specificity, then order.

screens.body:
Specificity is a score. Count the selector's parts: each id is worth 100, each class 10, each element 1.

#nav .link = one id + one class = 110. .card p = one class + one element = 11. p = just 1.

Higher score wins, no matter where the rules sit in the file. It's not a real decimal system, but the math works for comparing.
screens.heading: Specificity scoring

screens.body:
When two rules have the SAME specificity, the later one in the stylesheet wins. That's the "cascade" part of the name — styles flow down and later rules override earlier ones.

This is why stylesheet order matters: your custom styles go AFTER library styles, so yours win the ties.

Same score? Scroll down — the last one standing takes it.

options: The later rule in the file
The earlier rule in the file
check.question: Two rules, same specificity, both set color. Winner?

code.snippet:
p { color: red; }
p { color: blue; } /* same score — this wins */

screens.heading: Order breaks ties

screens.body:
!important is the cheat code: color: red !important; beats everything, including inline styles and higher specificity.

It feels powerful, and that's the trap. Sprinkle !important around and soon nothing can override anything — debugging becomes a nightmare.

Rule of thumb: fix the specificity instead. Save !important for true emergencies, like overriding third-party code you can't edit.

options: It beats all normal rules, even inline styles
It makes the style load faster
check.question: What does !important do?

screens.heading: !important: the cheat code
screens.keyPoint: !important beats everything. Use it almost never.

screens.body:
Inline styles (style="color: green;") beat any stylesheet selector — even an id. The browser treats them as ultra-specific.

But !important in a stylesheet still beats an inline style. That's the full pecking order: !important > inline > id > class > element.

This is also why inline styles are hard to override later — another reason to prefer classes.

screens.heading: Inline styles win (almost)
screens.keyPoint: Inline beats selectors; only !important beats inline.

screens.body:
Some properties pass down to children automatically — this is inheritance. Set color or font-family on body and the whole page picks it up.

Not everything inherits: margins, padding, and borders do NOT pass down. Each box keeps its own.

You can force it with the inherit keyword: color: inherit; explicitly takes the parent's value.
screens.heading: Inheritance: kids borrow from parents
screens.keyPoint: Text styles inherit. Box styles don't.

screens.body:
When a style won't apply, debug like this: open devtools, inspect the element, and look at which rules are struck through.

Struck-through = a higher-specificity rule beat it. That's your answer, right there.

If your selector needs three ids and !important to work, simplify instead — flat, class-based selectors are easier to override and easier to read.

options: A struck-through rule lost to a more specific one
A struck-through rule has a typo
A struck-through rule is loading slowly
check.question: In devtools, what does a struck-through rule mean?

screens.heading: Debugging conflicts
screens.keyPoint: Devtools strikethrough = outscored. Keep selectors flat.
